Formulation  
Patient presents with anxiety related to acute right knee pain and mechanical symptoms likely secondary to overuse injury during marathon training. Predisposing factors include a recent history of sports-related minor trauma (ice hockey injury), and active intensive physical activity. Precipitating factors include increase in running mileage, resulting in knee pain and intermittent clicking sensations, with transient toe tingling possibly related to local nerve irritation or vascular changes. Perpetuating factors include continued training despite pain and anxiety regarding possible ligament damage. Protective factors include engagement in care, willingness to modify activity, and compliance with symptom management. No significant psychiatric history or risk factors identified.  

Mental Health Care Plan Details  

Principal Problem: Anxiety related to knee injury concerns  
- Patient Goal(s):  
  • Reduce anxiety related to knee symptoms  
  • Resume marathon training safely without worsening injury  
- Clinical Goal(s):  
  • Provide symptom management and assessment to clarify diagnosis  
  • Facilitate appropriate referral and reduce anxiety through education  
- Actions (Patient):  
  • Follow advice to reduce running intensity while symptomatic  
  • Use prescribed anti-inflammatory medication as directed  
  • Attend physiotherapy assessment as scheduled  
  • Monitor for symptoms of swelling, heat, redness, fever, or locked knee and seek urgent care if these occur  
- Actions (Clinician/GP):  
  • Prescribe stronger anti-inflammatory medication (details not documented)  
  • Refer patient to physiotherapist for knee assessment  
  • Provide education on injury management and signs requiring urgent care  
  • Arrange follow-up or clinic assessment if symptoms persist or worsen

- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Persistent swelling, heat, redness of knee, fever, knee locking or inability to bend/extend  
- Coping Strategies: Ice therapy, activity modification, using medication appropriately, early help-seeking behavior
